utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Morning ladies and gentlemen. We are back in full force this morning. Can we have the appearances, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Dixon, Ms. McHenry and Mr. Khan for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic, counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic, together with my colleague, Eugene O'Sullivan, a professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour; I am Olujic, Defence counsel of Mr. Zdravko Mucic, together with my colleague, Mr. Michael Greaves. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honour, I am Mr. Karabdic, counsel for Mr. Delic. Mr. Delic is also represented by my colleague, Mr. Thomas Moran from Huston, Texas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honour, I am John Ackerman and I appear here with Cynthia McMurrey on behalf of Esad Landzo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Moran, you are still cross-examining.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, if you give me a second while he is coming in, to organise myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind the witness that he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am so reminded. DR. GOW (continued)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Gow. Did you have a good weekend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a pleasant weekend, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you go home or were you here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I wish I could, I am jealous. I have got a couple more documents I would like to let you have with a little help from the usher, three more documents and we will talk about them in just a -- let us get them passed out. (Handed). Professor, if you are looking at the first one, the document number is S/23900, I am going to refer you to paragraphs 1 and paragraphs 24 in a second, so... Okay, if I could have the exhibit numbers on these?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first one is document D20/3, the second one D21/3, and the third one, D22/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Thank you very much. Professor, the first one in D20/3 which is the document dated 12 May, I refer you to paragraph 1, right after the footnote 1. There is a statement by the Secretary-General: "Mr. Goulding was in Yugoslavia (a term which for the purposes of the present report is used to signify the Republics of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia)." Would you not agree with me that that is an indication that the Secretary-General agrees with your feeling, that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had ceased to exist by 12 May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that it is my feeling that it ceased to exist, but certainly my judgement that it ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your judgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that there is little doubt that for most people that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And if you look at paragraph 24 you will see the phrase, "the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia". Again, would you agree with me that that is an indication that the Secretary-General agrees with you that the SFRY had ceased to exist by that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that can be taken as an acknowledgement that the SFRY had ceased to exist by that date, although, as we were discussing on Friday, we had a number of similar cases. That does not necessarily mean that all the issues are tidied up. It is the difference between a dead body and the estate being sorted out for many years afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that. The next document is D/21/3...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which is which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: 27 July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I call your attention to paragraph 19 first. Again, we are talking about the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and here we are talking about international borders between Serbia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think... I think I follow your drift, and in general I think you are right, but I think that you have actually phrased it incorrectly because this question about the international borders is the international borders within the protected area of Croatia in the previous sentence, rather than a direct reference to Serbia because, of course, in Belgrade's and the outside world's terms generally the international border would not be with Yugoslavia but with the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Right. That would indicate again that there is a new nation floating around out there, the FRY that has international borders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take that as recognition of the fact that the declaration we referred to in the previous document of 27 April has taken place and that as a matter of fact the existence of Serbia Montenegro as a common entity has been accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And now let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But without prejudice to the legal issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. Let me direct your attention to D/22/3. Now, just so you know what this is and where this came from, there is a volume that is published by the United Nations every year called, "Resolutions and Decisions of the Security Council", and what I did was copy the front page so you knew where it came from and then copied various pages in between. It is not, believe me, a full copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have no problems with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just as a matter of interest, what is it that is deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It says, "official record", and it is not deleted, it was highlighted on the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Such is technology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, just so you know, there is one depositories library for the United Nations where I come from and this came from their library. Let me direct your attention to page 22 in here. On page 22, down at the bottom, or excuse me, in the right-hand column, there is a paragraph about halfway down which says: "At the same meeting, following consultations held earlier with members of the Security Council, the President made the following statement." Have you found that? I direct your attention to the following portions of the statement, where the President of the Security Council, after conversing with the members of the Council, talked about centres within the territory of the Former Yugoslavia and especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina; again, would that not lend support to your position that by the date of this, which would be 4 August 1992, that the Security Council had found that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had ceased to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the earlier documents, I mean, the 4th August series of documents that we have seen before that confirm that by that date the judgement was that the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia had ceased to exist as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And again on page 25, Resolution 771, there is expressing "grave alarm", that paragraph, again, the Former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the form, "Former Yugoslavia", appears, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, there is no doubt in your mind as an expert in the politics of the former Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the areas that grew out -- the states that grew out of it, that the Socialist Federal Republic ceased to exist as a nation, as a state, on April 27th 1992, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be my view. As I said, many times, at the latest. There was a process beginning in my judgement from 15th May when the Federation ceased to function. Now, that could -- depending on the analogy I used earlier could be that that was when it was kind of -- when the body died, 27th April is when it was pronounced clinically dead, and after that there was a post mortem and then, continuing to this day, testations about the estate, including who gets what in the assets and what to do with the people. I mean, some of the issues, if I may be presumptuous, I assume from this that this relates to the questions of citizenship?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You are exactly right. We will get to that in a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, which was one of the issues left to be decided, in the declaration you showed me on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What, the declaration of April 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which said kind of until these are finally decided, the SFRY -- the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, kind of something like continues to extend...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Comparable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this kind of thing, until it is finally decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure, but in fact when it comes to nationality, you have testified in the Tadic trial that the Republic of -- or the FRY and Republic of Serbia, never in any sense claimed that it had -- that the Serbs were living outside the borders of the FRY were nationals of the FRY, as I recall. Did you not testify something along those lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall precisely what I testified any more. Maybe if you have some specific reference I could be clear about what it is that I might have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. You said, one of the areas where I have a note is, there was a question asked by Judge McDonald, and she said: "I am very concerned about how Serb people consider themselves, what state they consider themselves belonging to, and various other Republics." And you responded: "None of the constitutional provisions, nor indeed any of the constitutional documents to which we have made reference so far give any indication of a responsibility of the Republic of Serbia or the JNA for Serb people specifically outside the Republic of Serbia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was an accurate statement. It could be amended by the discussion that we just had, reference to the document on FRY I am not sure how substantially it would amend the judgement. It is a distinction, again, between the formal technical position as set down in some of those documents and of course recognising in the character of the way the Communist political -- the Communist politics worked, that a lot of the time you had to have this kind of mode of deception to disguise what your actual position was, but that was the formal position, as per that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: In fact, that is consistent with article 17 of the constitution of the FRY, which we read Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not recall if it was article 17, but yes, it is consistent with material contained in that constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And in fact, if I were to tell you that the FRY did not pass any kind of citizenship law until 1996, and that that gave FRY nationality to all persons who were nationals of the SFRY and citizens of Serbia or Montenegro on 27 April 1992, you would not disagree with that, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would find it hard to disagree with it in the absence of alternative material, and I do not profess to be an expert in these matters, but I would point out that it was my understanding that there were steps taken in 1993, and at a later date which might well have been in 1996, both of which regulated the issues of passports linked to citizenship and that perhaps the 1996 law is the one which makes it no longer possible for people who were not citizens of Serbia or Montenegro at that time to become so, but in the interim certainly there were people who were citizens of other Republics who did, or who were treated as. I mean, for example, I think one of the former cases here, General Dukic, which case was set aside. General Dukic, as I understand it, was from Bosnia, as a Serb, but was an FRY citizen in Belgrade, so there are degrees of ambiguity. Again, part of this process of sorting out the elements in the period afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, by the way, just so that you know the source of that statement I made, it is the third report on nationality in relation to the succession of states from the International Law Commission and it is dated 28 February of last year. Coming back to the same subject, there is absolutely no question in your mind, is there, that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia and Montenegro are different legal entities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be cautious both as a non- -- I would be cautious in passing a judgement on that question, first because I am a non-lawyer, and secondly because it is an outstanding issue as part of the succession talks, so I would have thought as a matter of fact, both legal and political, that is not yet confirmed, but I would say as a political fact that the SFRY and the FRY are not the same political entity, and that, because that is the case, is why Belgrade is laying claim to be the sole legal inheritor of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Going to another -- by the way, that has never been accepted by anybody, has it? It has never been accepted, for instance, by the United Nations, that the FRY is the sole successor state to the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would hesitate to say it has not been accepted by anybody. I am not aware of its having been accepted by anybody. It is certainly not accepted by the parties to the succession talks, and it is not accepted in -- it is not accepted to the extent of the FRY's being admitted to full membership of the United Nations. One of the documents you had the other day referred to this, the question that, I think, one of the documents you showed me the other day? I think it was on something I have seen and maybe if not maybe it is something you are going to show to me. I mean it was one of the documents that I saw on Friday, either from you or the Prosecutor's Office, making precisely the point that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could not automatically be seen as sole legal successor and inherit the seat of the SFRY, that it would have to apply for membership.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually, that would be Resolution 777 which is on page 34 of that document in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, let us switch to a different topic. You testified when Mr. Ackerman was talking to you, and my notes say it is something along the lines that your knowledge of the Konjic area, the specifics of what went on in the Konjic area were relatively limited. Is that because, and I am not trying to denigrate anything that happened there, but that in any war there are going to be some areas that are essentially a backwater, where important events as they effect history and the war itself are not occurring. Is that what Konjic was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whether it was a backwater or not, I had not really considered before. It is conceivable that it could be interpreted in that way. I am not sure that I would or would not, without giving it greater reflection. I think what I would stress is that in making that comment to Mr. Ackerman I was recognising that I have a degree of expertise which operates principally at the strategic operational level, and what you are talking about in Konjic is, as in any other specific location, a tactical situation and therefore I would see my role as matching that which I know about the overall strategic operational situation to material which I may be able to use regarding an area like Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And in fact one of the things you said to Mr. Ackerman was, the real basis of your knowledge is, I think, the exact quote is, "material I looked at here". I presume that is material shown to you by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: What kinds of things did they show you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The kinds of documents that we have been discussing in the course of giving testimony, documents which I think, as I recall from before Christmas, Mr. Ackerman at some length raised the question of what were these documents and I think the Prosecutor pointed out that these were documents which had already been in evidence and had been used in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I think I seem also to recall that I made the point that whilst I had been given several bundles of the documents which had been used I had done my best to skim through and to try to identify things which, for the purposes of what I was being asked to testify to, might be of use. And I can quite readily admit that I have not exhaustively looked at all those bundles of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I do not think any expert witness in the world ever has, and I am proud of you for being honest enough, for being one of the few experts who will admit that. Did they show you some transcripts and testimony from some generals of the Bosnian army, Generals Divjak and Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did and I think we discussed this with Mr. Ackerman before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. When you were talking to him Friday, you were talking about chains of command and that it was not what you would expect in the -- in a regular armed force. I take it that is because at least the Bosnian army in the period we are talking about, May through August, September, October, of 1992, was in the process of forming and chains of command were pretty murky at best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that would be consistent with what I said before Christmas. It was a degree of -- it was a degree in which the process of forming an overall regular armed force was taking place on the part of the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that in that process there was always a degree of improvisation in some areas, but I think that still does not take away the point that within areas there would be degrees of command responsibility. There were structures that they were relying on, the elements of the Patriotic League, the nascent elements of the army linked between Patriotic League and Territorial Defence forces, the provisions of the old defence system, so there were elements, but the point I would make is that it was not a fully coherent regular command chain that you would see, for example, in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But it surely is not what you would see in the Dutch army. There are not the same kinds of little boxes for tables of organisation and things like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would make a distinction between the tables of organisation, because I suspect that people did have tables of organisation, but for some time, say, in the period towards the autumn of 1992, the boxes and the tables of organisation did not correspond with much of the reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: They did not. And in fact, two Bosnian generals who were on the scene at the appropriate -- at the times we are talking about, the May through December 1992 period, were to have looked at documents and looked at various things and based on their own experience said that they would be unable to say who commanded what, or -- the exact extent of the commander's authority, based on what they had within given and what they saw while they were there, they probably would be pretty right about that, would they not, that they could not tell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would find that -- I would find it hard to make a firm judgement, without knowing, looking precisely at the example. I think it is reasonable that they would have some sense of the degree to which command authority would run in a particular area. It is not inconceivable that they might -- kind of the question raised on Friday -- have self-interest in presenting things in a certain way as well. I am quite happy with my own judgement, which is that there were degrees of authority being exercised and that there was a formal command authority which was emerging, and in reference to this particular case, that from a certain date it can be said that there was a formal command authority position, but that is... sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, no, that is fine. Another thing you talked about, and this was back before Christmas, was the term, "coordinator", and if we can remember back that far...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I cannot remember what I had for lunch yesterday, so I understand where you are at, but you used an example with the term, "coordinator", comparing it to a position in the British army in the special operations executive during the war. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. I recall there was quite some discussion about the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And no army I am familiar with has a title, "coordinator". You may have various different things but you tend not to have coordinators. That seems to me to be kind of an ad hoc position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is the point I was making precisely before Christmas, that it was not a normal, regular function, it was something which would only emerge in specific circumstances, and would be a role designed to meet those specific circumstances, so yes, ad hoc -- precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And without knowing the exact circumstances and the exact duties given to that coordinator, be it to your colonel in the special operations executive, or someone in -- pick an army. You would not know exactly what his duties, powers or authorities would be, would you? All you know would be the title.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you would know the title and as I am sure I must have said in testimony before Christmas, the important thing is that if the coordinator is to have a meaningful role, then it has to be somebody who is able to have full knowledge and authority in circumstances where otherwise the specifics of the situation mean that the regular command chain is not going to operate, or there is not a regular command chain, it is an unusual, ad hoc situation. It is somebody who has the ability to be sure that all sides -- I mean the Hackett case, I mentioned the private armies, they would all talk to him, he would know everything that was going on and therefore would be able to use his personal authority to say, "you do this, you do not do that", and I think that is the essence of what I was trying to get across. The Hackett idea was an image. It is an analogy, rather like I was saying before about the dead body and the estate being sorted out afterwards. It is not to say that there is a precise correlation, but that within it, if the term means anything, then it means somebody who has the abilities to deal with all parties concerned within that same broad site and would do so on the basis of having full knowledge and authority with those parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you have absolutely no idea -- well, let me back off. If two generals in the Bosnian army said they had no idea what the powers and authorities of a coordinator were --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I do not think we are assisted by these generalisations. I think if counsel wants to draw Dr. Gow's attention to what the General said, it would assist everybody if he could go to precisely the part of the evidence that he is referring to, and to put that to the witness. I mean, these generalisation lead us nowhere. I think it just leads to done confusion and in my submission, your Honours, it would be much better, if counsel wants to compare what the Generals said and wants to put that to Dr. Gow, then I would ask him to go to the specific part of the transcript and to read that transcript to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, your Honour, I am not attempting to impeach either General Pasalic, General Divjak or Dr. Gow with the statements that the other one had. What I am trying to get at is who was more likely to know specific powers and specific duties of people. Two general officers on the scene, or a very learned professor from the United Kingdom who, basically all he knows is what he has read. Is that a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is not the point, your Honour. The point is that there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Actually, have you established that none of these witnesses has been able to tell who a coordinator is within the structure and the witness himself has not been able to tell you. I do not know what you are looking for here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, you have reached the point that I was getting to. I do not need to ask any more questions along that line and if I can --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am quite happy to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think that the question has been answered to the court's satisfaction. Let me go through my note and see if there is anything else I would like to ask you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, if I may...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, unless you still have any confusion in your mind, let us hear what you think, what your answer is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have clarity in my mind as far as, as far as is possible in these circumstances and maybe if I can assist in sorting out the confusion, I think you need to be clear first that the term, "coordinator", had no precedent as far as I am aware in the Yugoslav military context, but therefore you could not expect anybody, necessarily, in the Yugoslav context, a Bosnian context, to have any knowledge of what, "coordinator", would mean. It would therefore not surprise me in the slightest to find Generals Divjak or Pasalic or any others saying, "Well, I have never come across this term before and I could not tell you exactly what it contained", I think it is possible to say that the term does have relevance and as far as I understand it, the term was adopted at the local level and being adopted at the local level it presents some questions, what can it mean, and what I am putting to you is that what it can mean is something of this kind, because it is that -- that is the way in which it would make sense, and I would say no more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It can mean something different, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that it has to -- if it means anything, if it has real content in meaning, then it would have to be based on full knowledge and authority and my impression is that that is, as I described, I think, before Christmas, from reading the things that I have seen, that, for example, Mr. Delalic did have a degree of personal authority you could get on. He could talk to the Croats and he could talk to his own people. It was useful in that way. He had money, he could do things, and I think in a sense that is where this derives from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But you do not know what the job description was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the job description was, as far as I recall from seeing things, was to procure arms, to coordinate between the HVO and the various Territorial Defence paramilitary Muslim groups, within that context, to make sure that people were all -- that lines between them were clear, that supplies as far as possible were available, and I think all if that is what you see confirmed when he becomes appointed as the tactical group commander in the first instance for the specifically assigned units and then in the quite unusual measure for all units in the Konjic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, if two general officers from the Bosnian army said they looked at the same orders you looked at and did not know what he commanded, you would not disagree with them, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot disagree with what they say. If they say they do not know something then presumably they do not know something, and I am not sure what they would mean if they were to have said that they did not know. It does seem to me that if you see a document saying that all units within a specified territorial -- a specific delineated territory are under one person's command, and it is an order from the central command in Sarajevo, then that seems reasonable to suppose that all units in that sector are under that person's command. But of course, against that, as I pointed out, the realities of command authority also were that sometimes there was an apparent degree of insubordination within that structure, as I pointed out. These apparent arguments with Ramic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure. It was -- the lines of authority were murky or muddled to say the least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the lines of authority were fairly clear. I think in this case one of the individuals was bucking the system a little bit, but that certainly is an impression, I cannot be certain about that because I do not have enough information, just an impression from the things that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it is clear from within that that the authority rested with the commanding officer, and that the problem was not that he did not have the authority, but sometimes getting things done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are getting a little confused now. Now, there are two situations. The situation when the gentleman was a coordinator, and the situation when he became a commander. Now, what all the generals have consistently said was that a coordinator had no command, as far as they were aware. This is what they have all said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know whether that is also what you believe, from your analysis of the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- let me try to be clear about this, that what I have been saying is that coordinator is not -- it is not a normal position and it is not a command function in a normal sense, but to be a coordinator would require some of the qualities that would be present in an officer commanding, that is to say full knowledge of what is going on, and to have the authority to get things done, but not in the terms of a formal regularised command structure which has, for example, the back-up of military law behind it to penalise those who disobey. I think it is a degree of personal authority. My impression is that when Mr. Delalic is made commander in the area, it is precisely because, de facto, he has already been providing that role whilst designated coordinator but the term, "coordinator", is in part because of the ad hoc nature of the situation, that it has been improvised and in part because of the relationship with the HVO, it simply would not have been acceptable to appoint him and name him as commander because of the relationship between the Croats and the Muslims in the area as they were trying to coordinate joint defence operations. That is the impression that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Doctor, when you say, "personal authority", but it is not part of the command, the formal chain of command, would it be fair to say, to substitute the word, "influence", or something along that line where someone, rather than having the ability to court martial people and do whatever military commanders do, he just does it on his personal influence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The kinds of things that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that would be part of what I am saying, that he does not have -- precisely. He does not have the ability to court martial people for not doing things, but he does have the positive ability through what might be influence, might be money, well money as a form of influence in that case, but whatever, to arrange things so that people are doing those -- carrying out activities which are more or less consistent, going in the same broad direction, rather than crossing lines, doing things which would be counter-productive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Convince, cajole, negotiate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought all of those are part of the everyday life of an officer commanding and would be part of this role as well. I mean, a lot of it is based on character and personal authority. That is why people get to be officers commanding within the formal structures of an armed force as well because they show that they can -- they have qualities of leadership, organisation, even intuition, whatever. Those are the qualities which are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: But your normal officer commanding, the commanding officer of the whatever infantry battalion has formal structures, where you are saying this coordinator probably did not. It was more of a ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have acknowledged that -- several times -- that it was not a formal position in the sense of a regular armed force and part of the command hierarchy. I mean, it was a formal position in that it was designated by the presidents -- by the chairman of the local war presidency, so politically it was a formal position but it is not one within that command hierarchy of an armed force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. I pass the witness, your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May it please the court, thank you. Good morning, Dr. Gow. My name is Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. As I happen to be the last among the counsel to do the cross-examination, there are not many questions left for me to put to you that you have not already discussed. You will forgive me if, in the interests of clarification, I may go back to certain issues that have already been looked into, but which may not be quite clear to me as regards your understanding of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will forgive you anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that you took a doctorate on a thesis about Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure I did, if I was asked, but it is the case anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And on a number of occasions in response to questions put by the Prosecution, and my colleagues, you also said that in the last few years and on Friday you said for at least fifteen years, you have been focusing your studies on the military and political conditions in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Broadly that is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And today, again, you stated that it was your position that the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was the last to cease to exist, that is on the 27th April 1992, on the day when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed. Is it true, Dr. Gow, that on that date when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was proclaimed, the assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia passed a constitution in which it indicated its official name, that is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Was that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware, and in the course of the cross-examination you were shown a number of documents to that effect, that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as of that day, called itself by that new name, that is the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the case, although we also saw some documents which showed that, as was much of the discussion earlier on, some issues continued. I was shown documents from Blanko Kostic where he was still using the language and speaking as though the old structures still existed but yes, formally that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have also stated your opinion on a number of Security Council resolutions, one of which was the Resolution of May 15th 1992. It is Resolution number 752. In that connection I should like to ask you, since I am certain that you are very familiar with its contents, could you confirm that by this Resolution of 15th May it was clearly asserted that the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army and elements of the Croatian army should withdraw from the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Was that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was prescribed by point 3 of that Resolution, whereas point 4 provided also that the forces that would not withdraw had to be placed under the control, under the authority, of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think to be correct, both elements are contained within paragraph 4 which reads: "Demands also that those units of the Yugoslav People's Army and elements of the Croatian army now in Bosnia Herzegovina must either be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina." But, I mean, taken together, the essential point is that units should be withdrawn or subject to the authority of the Bosnian government.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And paragraph 5 says that all irregular forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina have to be disarmed and disbanded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document has already been admitted into evidence, so there is no need for me to tender it. However, in connection with questions relating to this case, I should like to ask you whether you are aware that all the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from the facilities in the town of Konjic by May 12th 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that I know that, because I no longer recall. I do recall, without the specific date, I recall that JNA units withdrew at a relatively early stage in the armed conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Konjic area and that this was treated as one of the initial big successes of the local defence courses, because precisely because the JNA had been, had withdrawn from barracks under control, and in one of the rare cases had withdrawn and left behind various forms of equipment and munitions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you testified to having seen many documents given to you by the Prosecution, then you could have found this statement in those documents, that is that after May 12th there were no remaining JNA forces in Konjic, so could you please confirm that, that this was certainly done before the deadline given by the main headquarters of the army of -- main headquarters of the JNA, that is before the deadline set by them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the date was 12th May 1991, then that -- then it would not have been the case that it was before the order which was on 4th May, but it would have been the case that that was completed before the completion, that the prescribed completion date on the 19th of May, so it was after the order, if it was the date. I have to say that I have looked at some of these documents in the autumn, and I am perhaps too far away from them to remember precise dates any more, but as long as nobody else contests the date, I am happy that that was the one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the benefit of the transcript, Dr. Gow, I have been told that you said that by 12th or rather the 19th May 1991; perhaps this was a slip, either on your part or on the part of the interpreters, but the correct date is 1992, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, yes. It was my mistake. I did say 1991 just now. I now hear it, now you point out. Excuse me, I meant 1992. You are quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to you, Dr. Gow, since several documents were commented on, D21, D22/3, so I would like to verify whether these documents have been admitted into evidence as they were tendered by my learned friend. These were documents that Professor Gow discussed with my colleague Thomas Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As far as I know, your Honour, they have not been admitted -- your Honours, I was going to comment on that. I do not think that they were tendered. I do not have any objection, but I query whether Mr. Moran seeks to tender the whole contents of the documents. There are, in some cases, many pages in excess of anything that he referred to, and I think, your Honour, that it is appropriate that only those parts of the documents to which he took Dr. Gow should be tendered in evidence, unless Mr. Moran would argue that the rest of it should be tendered. It seems to me that the parts that Dr. Gow were taken to should be admitted. I have no objection to that, but I do, at this stage, provisionally object to the rest of the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, they are Resolutions of the Security Council, and they are public documents. We can take judicial notice of them in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours can do that; except that I do not know to what other part of the documents they would seek to be used and it seems to me that, unless Mr. Moran would care to lay a foundation for the balance of them, then it is appropriate that only those parts of it which are referred to by Dr. Gow and referred to him by Mr. Moran should be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well your Honour, first, I did forget to tender them and I apologise to the Tribunal for that, and I will tender them, move them into evidence, and I would also ask the Trial Chamber to take judicial notice of them, as public documents of either the Secretary-General or of the Security Council which, of course, is the body that created the Tribunal, and is the superior body to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, I do not really want to make a big issue out of this, but it seems to me that if your Honours are going to take judicial notice then there is no need to tender them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually what constitutes international law are these things. This, I think, constitutes international law. It is material, in considering what is international law in this situation, I do not think we really care whether you tender them or not. Even if we found them ourselves we could have used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not offering them for the truth of the matter asserted there, I am just offering them that they are documents of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They are public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, and that is all that they are being offered for. That is what the public documents say, not that the statements of fact made therein are true and correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, on that basis I withdraw any objection I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, documents D20, and the others have been admitted, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will formally admit them. I think they should -- through you, they can still come.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Dr. Gow, I apologise once again for this short break. However, I should like to discuss with you some other issues. Since you specialise in political and military issues, beyond the territory of the Former Yugoslavia as well, I would like to ask you whether you are aware that in most European countries there is a prohibition on political organisation and activities of the political parties of other countries. For example, in England, the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, or the Serb Socialist Party, et cetera. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say that I think in the United Kingdom, whilst there would be -- would have previously been a proscription on membership, not only on membership of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union but possibly within the Communist Party of Great Britain within the armed forces, in general there is no proscription on membership of political parties and I think there would be no political question. I think the question just has not arisen as to whether it should be a political party from one country or many others, in other countries that proscript membership of a political party in Germany is quite normal and accepted as part of the civilianisation of the system. In some other countries it is wholly unacceptable. I think there is not one single message which you can give on that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, maybe my question was not clear enough. According to the constitution and the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina, even before the war and after the war there is a proscription on the operation on its territory of parties of third countries, regardless of the parties that are free to operate as parties of their country, so my question is, are you aware that what I know is true of my country, applies to the majority of other countries, that a political party of a third country is not allowed to engage in political activity or to be organised in a foreign country. That is something I am asking you to confirm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I hesitate to get bogged down in this, but I think it would depend on what you mean by, "political activity". Two things, I think, are the case. One is that in my own country and most other of the, say, for example, the EU member states of which I am aware, political activist members of parties from one country can go to another country and may make speeches/hold rallies. It is also the case that they might then separately also constitute a political party, for example, within the United Kingdom, which is somehow connected, a branch of that party, but which is a different party. Maybe I am struggling to understand what it is that you want from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Perhaps England is a wrong example. She is probably talking about the continent.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I am aware that is also the case in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: England has a different tradition altogether.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps my country -- I think I probably acknowledge that the UK generally is an exception to many rules but in this case, I think that the same applies when it comes to all the member states of the European Union. I would not state that categorically without looking into it closely, but I think it is in the nature of the European Union that something like that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: But are you aware of such a constitutional provision in the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is a separate question. I was not asked was I aware of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think they are tied together.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the question as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you are aware of that, then that question follows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Then yes, but I thought the question was, is the rest of Europe the same as Bosnia and Herzegovina, to which I was answering, "no", basically, but that is... sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the way that the question was put may have caused some confusion. May I try once again to establish understanding with what I am asking and what you are answering, namely, all that you have said, that someone with certain political convictions from England or another country may act in England or another country, I find that clear. I belong to a party in my state, and I come here in Holland and I am free to express my political convictions. But probably, according to the constitution and law of The Netherlands, I would not be allowed to form a branch of my party from Bosnia-Herzegovina here, to engage in political activity. So these are two different things. One thing is my human right and freedom to express and voice my political convictions wherever I wish, but I am asking, are you aware that this other thing is prohibited, that is for me to come here and form a party of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to act and be active here, and struggle for the aims of that party of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware that that is the case. I am not an expert in Netherlands electoral or party registration law. I would be surprise if it were not possible to organise a party for those purposes in The Netherlands, perhaps not for you as a non-citizen to do it but I am not sure what to say, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Though my question is, foreign citizens in a country would not be allowed to organise political parties of a foreign country. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, Dr. Gow, I think, has assisted as much as he possibly can. I think he has expressed his reservations and the extent of his knowledge on this, and I do not think -- I think it is flogging a dead horse to go any further on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I thank my learned colleague Mr. Niemann, but I think that Dr. Gow can answer, whether he is able to answer or not, any question put to him, so I would like to ask Mr. Gow to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have been making clear that I do not feel particularly qualified to answer these questions, but as far as I have understanding of them, I think it is not impossible. What I said before was that it would not certainly be the case that somebody, for example, yourself, you could come here and organise a political party. I do not know whether that would be the case or not. I would not exclude the possibility. I know of people in the United Kingdom, where that kind of thing has happened, so again, it is difficult. My familiarity is more with the electoral system in the UK than in The Netherlands, but...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I just want to know what counsel is about. Are you suggesting that because of the constitutional provision in Bosnia-Herzegovina no political party of a separate country can be established in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. A political party, shall we say, the De Gaullists of France cannot form a party in Bosnia-Herzegovina by French people, by foreign citizens. The citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina may form such a party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose, I do not see the difficulty in answering that question, whether, according to their constitution...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not see any difficulty in answering that question either, as I think I already have done, your Honour, which is to say that I would agree with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am satisfied. Thank you. However, let me ask you something else, which is probably much closer to your expertise. You know that in the majority of European countries there are many foreign citizens and would you agree that in most of those European countries cultural organisations of those foreigners is permitted. They may form clubs, cultural associations, and societies. You are familiar with that fact, I think, and can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: May we now go back to your work on questions related to the Former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. During the examination-in-chief and later you said that the testimony you gave before this Tribunal was based in the first place on your personal research, regarding the Former Yugoslavia, on your global understanding of world conditions in the world in Europe and in that area. Was that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose it must have been. Again, I do not recall precisely, but I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your views and knowledge was also based on the study of numerous documents, regulations, scientific scholarly publications, but third parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, when you were stating your views about conditions in Konjic you also said, as you did a moment ago when asked by my colleague, that your knowledge of the circumstances in Konjic was not the result of your prior personal investigations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is absolutely true. As I have said several times now in the course of testimony, I am not a specialist in Konjic, my degree of speciality is to do with military-political affairs across the territories of what was the SFRY. Konjic, like any other locality is only a question as far as I look into it with relevant material to see how it fits into that overall context. I am not here, as I understand it, I am not here as an investigator in the Konjic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as far as I was able to understand, so if that is correct, please confirm it, that most of your information about Konjic came from the material shown to you by the Prosecution, among which was the statement of Mr. Delalic. Would it be correct to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that would be correct, yes. I think -- yes. Certainly most of my knowledge of Konjic is based on those documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember in answer to a question by my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman, you mentioned one figure, one source regarding the quantity of armaments, that is a book by a Spanish author, of whom you did not have the precise data. However, conditions in Bosnia and Herzegovina were something that you studied at a much broader level so you had the opportunity to examine the regulations that preceded the war or that were passed after the outbreak of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen matters pertaining to official declarations, legislation, if that is what you are asking, yes. And for the record, the book was by Shabye Agere. Spelling, no doubt can be provided for the transcribers at another date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that in the Tadic case and probably also preparing yourself for this testimony, you studied most of the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. My question is, are you aware that already in April 1992 the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina passed a decree with the value of law, taking over the majority of the legislation of the former SFRY, establishing that they should be applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina until special regulations are adopted for particular areas, and this decree was published in the Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina, issue number 2. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not aware, I mean, I could not have told you that it was issue number 2, but I was aware that it took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then, Dr. Gow, you surely know that on April 8th 1992 a decree with validity of law was adopted, whereby the former Territorial Defence was reorganised, and made independent of the former Yugoslav People's Army, whereby it became the armed force of the new state. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with that. I think that was pursued as the mobilisation of the Territorial Defence on 4th April. The dates -- I think the date is probably right, but I am sure you would not be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that by that decree, certain authorisations in terms of the control and command of the Territorial Defence were conferred on the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina which, for a certain period of time, was, in fact, the supreme command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of the role of the Interior Ministry in the defence structures, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The translation that I received was the Interior Ministry, whereas my question was, are you aware that by this decree, passed on April 8th and published in Official Gazette number 1, authorising the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so it is either a wrong translation or we misunderstood one another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I was confused in the original question, both -- I mean, both statements, yes, the Ministry of Defence was authorised to organise a command, but there was a role within the structures for the Interior Ministry, but sorry, if I misunderstood the first question, then excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are here, so it is easy for us to correct any errors that may occur. Are you aware, Dr. Gow, that on the basis of this decree, which is actually law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Ministry of Defence, in accordance with its authorisations, conferred on it by this decree, passed or adopted instructions, temporary instructions on the subordination of district and municipal TO headquarters to the new headquarters of Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware of that, although going back to much of the earlier discussion, it is worth pointing out that this was a formal measure, and as I think I said in the original evidence it was many months before any of this began to have complete and real effect, and in the meantime there was this period of elements of improvisation, of trying to sort things out at different levels and using and relying on the old Territorial Defence practices and structures, so if there was -- in the absence of direct overall command from Sarajevo there would be local command and authority, for example, in this area, with the Konjic war presidency. So, broadly yes to the formal proposition, but bear in mind that the formal legislative position did not necessarily correspond with what was there in reality for some months. And of course, was subsequent to the decision to rename, as the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in, as I recall it was later in April or maybe in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could we now turn to the legal foundations for the establishment and structure of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then later we may go back to the actual situation in Konjic. In connection with these two documents that were officially published in the Official Gazette number 1, and these instructions, you are familiar with these documents, legal documents of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Do you know, Dr. Gow, that these provisional instructions, compiled by Dr. Divjak and issued by the Minister of Defence, Jerko Doko and which has been admitted into evidence, D122/1, stipulates that all municipal and district headquarters need to be subordinated to the republican headquarters of Territorial Defence and where no such district headquarters exist, that the municipal staffs should be directly subordinated to the republican headquarters of Territorial Defence. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not clear about the question by the end of it, if you could, would you mind repeating it?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have already confirmed that you are familiar with the fact that these documents were adopted. This document was drawn up by Colonel Divjak and issued by Defence Minister, Jerko Doko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, if you have looked at that document, do you know that that document requires the placing under the control of the republican staff all the municipal and republican staffs of Territorial Defence and that this document says that in cases when there are no district staffs, that the municipal staffs should be directly accountable to the republican staff. Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes I am, now I have understood clearly that, where a level of command structure is missing, then the local level should be directly responsible to the chief, to the general staff, yes. But again, in line with the provisions of the defence doctrine, if that is not available then the local authority will make decisions at its own initiative. That is how I would interpret the defence system.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So therefore your answer is that you are familiar with that. Dr. Gow, will you tell me, please, whether you know that this same piece of legislation established also that all patriotic and armed groups and forces need to be placed under the command of Territorial Defence staffs by April 15th 1992, and that precisely for this reason, this date is considered to be the date marking the establishment of the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take that to be the date marking the formation of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina as distinct from the formation, formal formation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which came slightly later but, if I understand these things correctly -- but the basic answer, with that minor qualification, is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I agree that you do not agree only with regard to the name, the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a name that was given subsequently. Thank you. Dr. Gow, you are also aware that in the development of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina a prominent place was played by decrees on defence and the armed forces adopted on May 15th 1992, and published in the Official Gazette, number 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. As I recall that would be the point at which I would say that was the point at which the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina formally took shape.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Dr. Gow, you would agree with me, that the development of the armed forces which later became the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was defined by legislation passed by the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of political fact, I understand it to have been established by legal measures, within the -- by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you now, Dr. Gow, are you aware that in mid-April, or, to be more precise, on 17th April 1992, a Municipal Assembly meeting was held in Konjic at which the former TO staff was reorganised as a new TO staff, to bring it in line with the provisions of these decrees that I referred to early on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that some action was taken at that stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, in actual fact, if that was indeed on the 17th April 1992, the military structure of the Territorial Defence and the defence forces of Konjic was brought in line with the instructions issued by the Minister of National Defence. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not want to speak too strongly on the matter in either direction. I think it was the case that some action was taken. Whether or not it was brought completely in line and what the implications of that would be, I think would be something about which we should exercise care. That is, formally some action was taken, but it does not mean that the full content of things being brought into line was achieved.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, Dr. Gow, you are not aware of the opposite being true. You do not know that everything was done, but you also do not know that what I have suggested was not done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what it was now that you suggested was done, in particular. I mean, I think it was just that I was being careful about the expression that you gave, which was, "brought into line with". And I would just say that that should not be interpreted as being a full establishment, i.e., not everything could be brought into line but action was taken regarding the steps to be taken, so something was done, but not necessarily all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, you could normally answer this question with greater precision, if you had the minutes from that meeting of the Municipal Assembly in Konjic. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would imagine that the minutes from the meeting in Konjic would give evidence of discussion and decisions taken, but still would not give you information actually on implementation, and I think some of the other evidence that we have discussed over the course of my giving testimony here indicates that there were areas of -- shall we say blurred areas, areas in which certain things were not yet clear, in which practical measures and authority was being worked out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Both of you are actually speaking out of context, because we do not know what those minutes of the meeting are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I am -- simply to say that hypothetically, even if we had the minutes right here in front of us, all they would tell us would be what went on at the meeting rather than what was implemented pursuant to the meeting, which I think is the point that I was making.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are probably not familiar with many of these documents that Dr. Gow is referring to, as I am not, but he is expressing many of his hypothetical views on the basis of things that he personally did not study, so I am going to try and be more precise. Would you think this would be an appropriate time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, by the time you return you might have organised your thoughts clearly as to where we are going to. So we will break now and return at 12 noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may continue Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Dr. Gow, before we continue, when you only wish to say, "yes", would you please state it so clearly, because I have noticed that in part of the transcript there were some nods that were not taken down, so if you would just please, when you confirm something, you also say so, by answering, "yes".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gladly. I think that I probably did, but maybe it was not registered. If there are any such points you want to take me back to, I am happy to revisit them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will review it and we will see if there are any unclear points, so we will get back to that if necessary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the record I said, "okay", there as well. I realise that had it did not sound here, so...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Dr. Gow, we left off when we talked about the last assembly meeting in Konjic in April of 1992. Do you know that in this assembly meeting it was concluded that all patriotic forces, that is the organised armed groups, that had to be put in service of the defence forces of the HVO and the MUP, which was in accordance with the decisions made by the republican bodies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I think I will have to ask you to repeat the question, because I think the translation may have been a bit muffled, I am getting two versions, so if you could, please...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Konjic parliament, the assembly, in this meeting of April 1992, concluded that all armed forces, all patriotic forces had to be, as of that moment, be placed under the command of the staff of the Territorial Defence, that is the -- under the command of the territorial forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is clearer and better, although this time there was no mention of MUP and other forces as well, which was making me unclear. Specifically, I cannot say here and now I am aware of that decision on that date, but it seems to me perfectly reasonable to say that that would have been taken and consistent with things that I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly Dr. Gow, you are familiar with the fact that only the SDS armed forces were the ones which did not place themselves under the control of the legal defence forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that the -- for present purposes we will call, "pro-SDS", elements did not put themselves under the command of the official authorities, and the official armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is also fair to point out that the HVO, the Croatian forces, only did so at a very formal level, in an initial attempt, but there was always a considerable degree of autonomy, and I suspect a degree of friction in this -- generally and in this specific area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you call this a reasonable decision of the assembly, and with respect to that, could you confirm, Dr. Gow, that after that date there are no independent or private or other uncontrolled groups in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I would not confirm that there were no independent or private or any of these other labels after that date. From that date, it was clearly the formal position that there should not be any, but as I was indicating earlier on, it is one thing to look at the decision taken, or the minutes of a meeting about a decision taken, and then to consider the time period in which the decision itself is implemented, so for some time to come, as I recall from a case in the autumn which came out in, I think it was "Dane", one of the Sarajevo newspapers about cases in which still, certainly in late 1992, possibly in early 1993, private armies, Muslim paramilitary groups were being held responsible for killing Serbs in the kind of north-west Sarajevo suburbs there, in the edge, I forget the precise detail, and this was coming out and was being condemned by the Bosnian government as the detail was emerging. So I think, I would make a distinction between the decision taken, and the period it takes fully to have everything integrated, and under control, as that, I think, would show.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what you know from the paper, "Dane", is what I know from my personal experience in Sarajevo at that time, and my own involvement in prosecuting this. So, I am not excluding your knowledge or questioning your knowledge about certain incidents in other areas, but do you know from any precise data that there were some such groups in Konjic who had not put themselves under the command of the armed forces of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I conclude from that which I have seen that there was not a precisely defined and clear situation in Konjic, that it was one which was evolving and one which, particularly because of the relationship with the HVO but also regarding elements within what people would call the Muslim or the Bosnian elements loyal clearly to the Bosnian government, there were still elements being sorted out. I do not see why there would be any problem in accepting that a decision made one day takes some time to have effect before everything is coherently arranged. I gave the example of Sarajevo simply to indicate one clear case which has emerged to show how, I think, throughout the country there would be such examples to be found.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I believe that you can agree with me that in this period, that is early on in the war, April 1992, and let us say, through the summer or fall of 1992, the defence forces of Konjic, that is the forces who were fighting for the liberation of the town, included the Territorial Defence, the HVO, and the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree that all of those were present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you do not have any reliable document on the basis of which it would -- which would show that apart from these defence forces there were some other private armed groups in the town of Konjic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my recollection that I saw materials indicating that there were such groups in the area. I do not have the specific recollection to mind. I would be happy to review documents and to indicate where that was the case, but...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you have not verified authenticity of any such document, provided you had some such document available to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not personally verified any of the documents, and as I think we have discussed previously, it was my understanding that these are documents which are either accepted in other cases or have been entered into evidence in this case, and at a minimum already given to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you some questions in a narrow area relating to the events before the events in Konjic that we are concerned with. In the Tadic case you testified on the basis of studying a number of decisions taken by the SDS in the 1991, and then later the SDS party in 1991, and in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is correct that I used a variety of documents including some SDS documents which related to the project to create the territory from Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., to form Republika Srpska to be separated from Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to request assistance to show Dr. Gow a document that has not been used previously in the proceedings. Could you please tell me how it is going to be marked?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D133/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I presume you are familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid to admit that I am not certain that I am. I do not recognise it, I might have seen it before, I am certainly aware of this decision on this date to implement it, and I have made reference to that in previous testimony. I cannot say for sure that I have not seen it, but it does not -- it is not immediately familiar to me. But I am very glad to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
