utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you can testify before this Trial Chamber that in the fall of 1992, after 1991, after the famous address of Radovan Karadzic, the parliament, the Serb population in Bosnia and Herzegovina was organised contrary to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina at that time. Are you familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure which fact I am being asked about, but if I may, I will state a number and hope that one of them is the one. I am familiar that in the autumn of 1991 Radovan Karadzic made some statements to the effect that you suggested. I am aware that in the autumn of 1991 the Serb autonomous regions mentioned here, and consistent with that statement were declared, so in either case I think I would agree, but I am not sure which one it is that you wanted from me. I might also point out that that decision built on the earlier measures taken in April 1991, to form associations of Serb, so-called associations of Serb municipalities, and this was a further step in that process. It was certainly judged by the third element of whether, do I agree with the fact, I am not sure if I could give a legal interpretation, but I can certainly say that it was a judgement of the constitutional court in Sarajevo that these were anti-constitutional or illegal measures, so I hope one of those three facts is the one you wanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You actually answered my next question, but I would still like you to look at the document and confirm that this was a document which, in fact, legally confirmed this decision to establish Serb autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would take a reservation on making the legal judgement regarding the document, but I would say, I would confirm that it is a document which confirms the political decision to create the autonomous regions in Bosnia and Herzegovina with the five regions indicated with some of their composition, or the composition at that stage. I would also confirm that if you go to paragraph 2 it makes clear that the intention is for these autonomous regions to be associated with Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection, with respect to this document, Dr. Gow, could you say that it is an incontrovertible that the town of Konjic is located in the part of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is called Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I think there may a little bit of a problem in the way the question comes through. Is Konjic -- if the question is, "is Konjic part of an area, Herzegovina", then as far as I understand the answer is, "yes". I am not sure with the reference in connection to this document, Konjic is not a place mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is, whether in point 1 of paragraph 3, which regulates the Serb autonomous region of Herzegovina, the town of Konjic is included.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in that case -- if the town of Konjic is not mentioned in that paragraph, although as I think I indicated in evidence-in-chief there were other documents where, on the basis of the number of representatives in the local municipality it was designated to be part of the Republika Srpska, or at least part of it would have been. There are arguments as to how realistic it was to assume it could be incorporated, given its demographic composition. Is that satisfactory?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is very satisfactory. I would just like to ask you further to maybe specify what you had explained more generally. In essence, does this decision of the assembly of the Serb people express a certain political position by which the town of Konjic was not supposed to be included in these territories of the autonomous province, Serb provinces and later Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that what you can say is that this document does not list Konjic as being one of the municipalities already part of the declared Serb autonomous regions. I do not think you can read into it necessarily anything about intent, and as I said, there is other material which indicates that it was considered that it might become part of the Republika Srpska, again, however unrealistic it might have been because of the demographic composition. But it was considered, although I do not think it makes any particular difference if you are considering the issue of armed conflict, because the armed conflict encompasses the whole of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whether it is intended to be part of one part or the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to tender this document now as defence exhibit. Is it accepted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no objection to it, except that it may have already been tendered in the Prosecution case. We are just checking, your Honours. Yes. There is no objection, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Admitted. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, you are probably familiar with the fact that in March of 1992 the assembly of Serb people of Konjic municipality adopted a decision on the Serb territories.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you then agree with me that the SDS of Konjic was practically adopting decisions apart from the SDS assembly at the republican level based on this document that we have just reviewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If judgement were to be made purely on the basis of that document, then you might well draw that conclusion. However, as I have indicated, there were other documents, including the SDS party instructions on how to organise, on the basis either of a majority Serb population within a municipality, or on the basis of the number of representatives in the Municipal Assembly, and that on the basis of that second category, Konjic was included within SDS, within the SDS framework for mobilisation for action. Therefore, the simple proposition, if you make the connection with this document, is you cannot draw that from this document, but if you are aware of other things, then you would see that there was an overall SDS -- that the overall SDS programme included Konjic within the frame of reference for action. I think I said already when I was giving evidence-in-chief that whilst I know that there was a decision to be made on the number of representatives in the Municipal Assembly I have no idea what number qualified, I have no idea what the number in Konjic was or what number would qualify for action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall your answers during the examination-in-chief, Dr. Gow, you pointed to some changes of the political position after the meeting of Borodan Karadzic after the meeting in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may well have done. I do not recall doing so, but if the question is asked in specific reference to the issue we were discussing immediately previously, then I think the answer is possibly no, because as I recall, the documents, I am talking about were from the period prior -- April or earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, I am one person in this courtroom to become familiar with the name of John Hackett, and I am very glad that I did so, because through that testimony I found out additional facts about this person from England. You used John Hackett to present to the Trial Chamber your own view what a coordinator, what a function of the coordinator might be. Have I summed up correctly, what you -- what your intention was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. My intention was to assist in clarifying what that role might be, what that term might mean and I used the example of Hackett during the Second World War. I have to say it is not purely and simply my own conclusion. I based on discussions with others, including senior military figures, about -- with whom I discussed the question of, you know, "how would you understand this, would this be a fair understanding". If I might, this might be a point, if your Honours permit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If you can explain --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to point out that in the break, because questions had been asked about the evidence of Generals Divjak and Pasalic, I did ask to be given the testimony just quickly to peruse. I am afraid I did not get to look at the Divjak but I already noted in the Pasalic that contrary to some of the views that were expressed, and I can confirm my own feeling, which is that they did not say that they accepted the coordinator meant nothing or that it was not a recognised, or that it was not something which they would understand, but simply that, as I had said before, consistent with what I had said, that it was not a formal recognised position, but that they could imagine the usefulness or rather Pasalic said that he could imagine the usefulness of such a role in a case where lines were unclear where something was involving, where there was a degree of improvisation, so I think just to be clear on that point, while we are talking about the issue of coordinators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you Dr. Gow, for having reminded yourself of what the general said, but as we were here present I think that the court and the rest of us are familiar with those facts. To go back to John Hackett, I wanted to ask you a few things that may be of use to all of us. Could you tell me, please, John Hackett was a respected citizen of England, even before the Second World War, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he was a scholar. It is hard to judge the degree to which he was respected, but yes. I mean, he was originally from Australia but he was a recognised scholar, a person of some respect, I suppose, yes, although I am not particularly qualified to judge the degree to which he was respected at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And he lived in England before the Second World War, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was a scholar at, I think, Oxford.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And through many years of life there he surely was very familiar with the conditions in England, and this probably served as a basis for him to be proposed to hold such a post.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that his familiarity with conditions in England or the UK as a whole are necessarily of particular relevance to his being given specific functions whilst serving in the armed forces. I mean, he was inducted. He was serving in the armed forces before he was given such a role, it just happened to be that at a certain point ad hoc, as Mr. Moran put it this morning, a situation emerged and in that ad hoc situation he was a person who could carry out that role.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but as a participant of the armed forces of England and someone familiar with those forces, he had sufficient knowledge of the conditions in the armed forces of England, because, after all, that is the basis for, as you said, the possibility of somebody being appointed to such a function.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the key things are first that he was a member of the armed forces, secondly, that whatever the existing character and structure of the British armed forces, there was a peculiar development taking place in the course of the Second World War regarding what I alluded to in evidence-in-chief as "private armies", that is the formation of what was later to become the special forces, and that in that evolving context where there were degrees of uncertainties where some individuals had decided that they would like to form their own small special units where others had been instructed to form small, special units, his role as coordinator was to bring all of that together, so I think the idea of the experience of the British armed forces is of limited value, because it was the British armed forces in new circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I gathered that, but regardless of his personal abilities, if he had just come from Australia and if he had never lived in England, and if he was not familiar with the armed forces, he would not have had a chance of being appointed to such an important position. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not quite sure, to be honest. In the situation of the Second World War and where new developments are taking place and there is a degree of improvisation, and given what I have said previously several times about the qualities required of a coordinator, there is a basic fact that he was present, but beyond that I think it can be said to be his qualities of being able fully to know, because of having the trust, respect, of those involved in the so-called "private armies", and the ability therefore to influence them to make suggestions and give directions on how best to proceed. There is nothing which necessarily says that he has to have had that experience previously. If I may give another example from the Second World War, one relevant to Bosnia and Herzegovina, a British conservative MP, Sir Fitzroy Maclean, a close friend of the Prime Minister, Winston Churchill, was chosen Churchill to go to be a special operations executive liaison officer with Tito and the partisans simply because he was judged by Churchill to be the best qualified person to do so, so I do not think the situation of being in that position and knowledge beforehand in the circumstances of some of the things happening in the Second World War necessarily means some of the things that you said had to be there, that some of the things you mentioned had to be there for that situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps, Dr. Gow, we are going outside our subject matter, certainly that Mr. Churchill, like any other statesman or civilian body may appoint somebody to carry out a certain task for him. Of course, General Maclean did not take over any of the obligations or responsibilities of Churchill. He just carried out the tasks assigned to him by Prime Minister Churchill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the same way that Hackett carried out those responsibilities which were due to him, not the responsibilities of Churchill either.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, speaking about John Hackett, you said that he was to have coordinated among the various armies which emerged in the structure of the English army, as you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand the question, yes, his role was to coordinate various small units which were evolving within the broader context of the British army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So his duty was not to coordinate the work of civilian authorities or certain armies, for instance, the municipality of London, and certain military structures or units. That was not his duty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I understand it that was not one of the tasks which he carried out, although I imagine had it been relevant to his situation, then it would have been, in the nature of something which is per ad hoc situations that you do those things which are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has probably shown you, Dr. Gow, the appointment, the document appointing Zejnil Delalic, and authorising him to coordinate between the war presidency as the civilian body and the defence forces. Are you familiar with that document of appointment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, the task assigned to this coordinator in Konjic differed from the one assigned to John Hackett.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it differed in its specific content, but I think that was clear some time ago when I was giving evidence-in-chief, and their Honours asked me some questions about the role of John Hackett. I think the essential thing always to bear in mind is the qualities inherent in a coordinator, full knowledge and authority, and the degree to which those qualities are put into effect, whatever the tasks in question might be, and recognising that those are similar qualities to be found to those found in an officer commanding, but are pertinent to a non- -- to a specific, or a peculiar situation in which normal structures do not apply, and I think the key point is that the comparative reference to Hackett is to show that in a situation where normal structures were not relevant, the role of coordinator was relevant, and I was making the allusion to try to understand the term "coordinator" in the Konjic context, to say that it was something which could be useful in that specific context and it would still have, when distilled, those same key elements and I take it from my refreshed reading of the evidence of General Pasalic that that was probably his judgement as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have no reliable source, nor are you aware whether there were any groups in Konjic that called themselves, "the Patriotic League", "the Green Berets", so you conveyed your thoughts on the basis of information that such groups did exist in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, as I said earlier, it was on the basis of references to, as I recall, at least two paramilitary groups operating in the Konjic area, and as I said earlier, if I am given a chance to revisit the documents that I have seen, I would be happy to identify where that was and to confirm it and if I am mistaken, to withdraw the opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, you do not recall at this point in time on the basis of which document you asserted that there were private armies or paramilitary groups in Konjic, after the 17th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case. I cannot point to this document and say, "that is the one". But, as I say, I am quite happy to look into this and to produce what it is that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that Mr. Zejnil Delalic lived for twenty years abroad before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am still aware that he spent some time living outside the SFRY, Bosnia and Herzegovina, prior to the dissolution and conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware that he came by chance to attend the funeral of his brother, just before the war, and that he stayed on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that he came to Bosnia at that stage for a funeral of his brother. That he -- I have no sense of whether -- of what degree of chance operated. Perhaps there was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware, Dr. Gow, that Zejnil Delalic was not a member of political parties.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Depending on precisely what you mean by that. It may well be that he was not a member of, by some technical definition that you might not offer, of a political party, but it is clear that he was a member of the SDA, at least from things that I have seen and I cannot tell you exactly what they are either, but I am happy to identify them, again, if it is desirable that I should do so, that he was a member of an association formed in Vienna of the SDA party from Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I would take that, other than in a technical sense as being membership of a political party, and I would also point out that prior to his coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina he was also a member of the organisation called Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of the examination-in-chief you referred to what Zejnil Delalic spoke about that in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that in that statement made in Scheveningen, Zejnil Delalic clearly stated that he was not a member of the SDA, and that he received a membership card of the Green Berets in the course of a celebration in 1994. Is that what you read in his statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that that is what he said in his statement, but also that the actual documents indicate membership of the Green Berets from an earlier date, and that the membership of the SDA is a moot point as to the technical definition of whether you regard being a member of the SDA Association in Vienna as being a member of the party. Obviously, he was not a member of the party in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I think to be a member of the SDA Association would reasonably be seen to be a member of the SDA, albeit, or a supporter of the SDA living abroad, if not a member of the party then a clear member of the supporter's club.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, your hypotheses are virtually just your interpretation of some of the documents shown to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure precisely which hypotheses you make reference to, but I think I would confirm, as I have done in many cases, that I draw my conclusions on the basis of the evidence available to me and my reading of it, which, in this particular case, includes materials provided by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though Zejnil Delalic said in the statement that you rely on that the Green Berets did not even exist in Konjic in 1992, and that the booklets, the cards were only issued in 1994, as is evident from that interview, so your conclusions can hardly be said to be based on reliable foundations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Personally I would regard it as being a reliable inference based on the existence of a membership card of the Green Berets from, as I recall, January 1991 or January 1990, certainly a date prior to his return to Bosnia and Herzegovina for the funeral of his brother, or the onset of armed hostilities. Now, I am sure this is more pertinently a matter for an investigator to have looked at, but as far as I have looked at this and I have integrated it in my overall understanding then I would say that that does seem to be the case, and whether or not the Green Berets were specifically formed in Konjic at that stage I am afraid I cannot say. My comment was on Mr. Delalic's membership of the Green Berets organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You assessed Mr. Delalic's influence also from the fact that he had assisted the defence with his own personal resources. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had drawn the inference from looking at some of the things he appeared to be doing and from reading some of the documents, in particular the documents saying that he would be doing things at his own expense, that one of the factors in his being able to play a role was that he had personal finance, and that he was prepared to put this at the disposal of the defence of Konjic specifically and I suppose Bosnia and Herzegovina more broadly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware, Dr. Gow, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the beginning of the war, thousands of citizens contributed funds to assist the Defence. Women were giving their jewellery, men, whatever they had, in order to provide the minimum conditions for defence in view of the sudden circumstances that arose.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that people in Bosnia and Herzegovina were making those contributions which they were able. I think the point I was making is that Mr. Delalic, as a seemingly wealthy businessman coming from outside, was in the immediate position of having reasonably substantial resources available to use, rather than small amounts to put in to an overall kitty and that is what gave him -- again, and I say this is only interpretation of the things that I see, I do not know this to be the case, but as an expert looking at the bits that I have seen, my interpretation would be that he did have specific personal wealth at that stage and in that particular situation he was prepared to put it to use for the defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and did so. But that is not to say that there were not other people in other areas who would do the same or that the people as a whole were not making contribution and committed to their own defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Gow, that more than 10 individuals in Konjic contributed much more and much more significant resources over a longer period of time than Mr. Zejnil Delalic did, and that this was nothing strange compared to people who contributed their factories, bakeries, petrol stations and so on. It was not unusual at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I absolutely recognise that there were many people who were making contribution. I think I did that in the previous answer. I would make the distinction between what you just put to me in terms of over a longer period, and the specific relevance of the resources which Mr. Delalic maybe had available in that specific period where there was an immediate need, but I would not want the whole understanding to turn on the question of the degree to which he used his own finance to play a role. As I have said, it was clearly the case that he was able, through his own personality, on the whole, to be able to influence people, and to play the kind of role which we discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in the course of the examination-in-chief, you spoke about the development of the armed forces, and as far as I understood you, you mentioned that there was the stage of coordinator, then tactical groups, then the specific role of tactical groups and finally the formation of cause. Did I understand well a short review of the things you discussed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With reference to developments in the Konjic area, yes. It may well have been that there were coordinators in the other areas, but use of the term "coordinator" has been discussed specifically with reference to Konjic and its surrounding region, but broadly, the understanding is correct, as I discussed the process of formation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about the formation of the tactical group in May. I think you can agree with me, if I say that it was formed on 14th May, and that its first commander was Mustafa Polutak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I would agree on that, yes. I always have difficulty remembering the dates unless I have been looking at them, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the headquarters of the tactical group 1 was in Pasarici, about 60 kilometres north of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that Zejnil Delalic, as a coordinator, was nominated on 18th May 1992, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is the case, yes. That is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think we can stop now, and reassemble at 2.30 for you to continue with your cross-examination. The Trial Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just to come back to what we talked about before we left off, before the break you confirmed that during the examination-in-chief you pointed out that a stage of development of the BH Army in the area of Konjic would be followed in such a way that there would be a coordinator, a tactical group and later an army corps. Then I asked you something which you confirmed, that the Tactical Group I was established on May 14. Is that correct? And that its commander was Mustafa Polutak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is what we were saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that Zejnil Delalic's coordinator was appointed on 18th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that confirms what we were saying this morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I believe that you can agree very easily on the date, on the fact that the 18th May is later than 14th May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that -- I do not see any problem in agree being that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that the sequence of phases in the situation in Konjic would start with the tactical group and then something was interrupted and then we come to the next phase. However, I am not trying to elicit your comment. I think this is something that can be simply inferred rather than to which you need to testify directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if I may I would just point out that I did not say that it was a phased sequence. I said that these were aspects of the evolving situation, and there would be a difference between a completely phased situation from one step to another and a state of flux in which a number of things were happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I must say that I am not an expert for military matters but listening to the generals and officers as well as the experts in this field such as you, I am learning, so I would just like you to confirm that my understanding of what you said is correct, that is that you confirmed before this Trial Chamber that the tactical groups in all continental armies are known as temporary formations with certain tactical tasks, and that they are formed for a particular time frame until such a task is executed. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is more or less a correct understanding. Tactical groups both in the old JNA and in other places are understood to be ad hoc temporary formations, usually a small number of units assigned for one of two types of purpose. One, a very specific purpose in designated operation and the other in an area of uncertainty and weakness where the mission is to do whatever you can.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if my understanding of what I have heard about tactical groups is correct, please confirm for me, is it true that in all armies, tactical groups are formed as temporary, either operational or manoeuvre units, whereas in the -- and that can also be done in the armies that are already established.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tactical groups can certainly be established where there are already existing armed forces established and again in that context it is to meet a specific need where the regular structures are not compatible with the tasks to be set. It is for a temporary period, but the period might not necessarily be defined. It might be defined by the task and when the task is accomplished then that period would be at an end, so temporary in the sense that it is not foreseen that it will be a permanent element in the structure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This morning we talked about regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by which it regulated its armed forces and the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Since you are familiar with these regulations you can certainly agree with me that in none of these regulations that we have mentioned neither the coordinator nor tactical group were foreseen as parts of the development of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can agree that we discussed the documents this morning, and that because neither of the functions you make reference to, either that of coordinator or that to be performed by a tactical group are part of the regular structure of the armed forces, the position of tactical groups, as far as I am aware, is not something which would usually be subject to legislation. It is something which would be a decision probably at an operational level, possibly at a tactical level, depending on a particular situation in the course of military operations. Sorry, if I may just make clear the last point, what I mean is that I would not expect to see it in legislation because it is not part of the structure, the normal arrangement for things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you would agree with me if I said that the law on the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina did foresee its own development and the need of establishing first brigades and then the corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was set out as a sequence of phases in the establishment and development of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would agree that that was the structure foreseen and the one upon which work was done to develop it, yes. But that work took time and in the meantime, there was this continuing state of evolution in which other things were relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We talked -- in fact you talked about it, you and I have not touched upon it yet, you said that Sarajevo was a major problem for the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is the blockade of the capital was a major problem for the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the very beginning. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall what I was saying was that the -- that in this phase which primarily we have under discussion between spring and autumn 1992, there was a specific objective for the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina to attempt to relieve the encirclement of Sarajevo and that some of operations, including those designated for the tactical groups, were geared towards that objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that the basic goal and the mission during this encirclement of Sarajevo in certain parts of Sarajevo area, part tactical groups were formed and the formation of a tactical force, of Tactical Group I was precisely to try to break the siege of the city of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I refer you to my last answer in which I think that is what I confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, during your testimony in examination-in-chief, while clarifying this period, you said that in Konjic there were about 2,000 members of the Territorial Defence during that period. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I recall saying, and I am not sure if this is exactly the same thing, but what I recall saying was that there should have been 2,000 members on the list for the Territorial Defence in the Konjic area, but a large number of them did not respond to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind you of this answer at page number 9,274 when you said that there were more -- where you stated the number of the members of the territorial unit, but my question to you is whether your view, that is your conclusion was based on documents offered to you by the Prosecution in addition to the documents found in possession of Mr. Delalic referring to the establishment of the tactical groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I am unable to answer that question because it is not clear to me which of the documents I have seen are those deriving from Mr. Delalic. I would have to appraise things on the basis of saying, "these are documents from Delalic and these are not", before I could be sure to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to request for assistance to show Dr. Gow the documents, the chart, which came from the Prosecution, and whether he based his views also on this particular chart. Could the document please be marked before we start?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D134/1.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you reviewed this document when you reviewed the documents given to you by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Quite possibly. It is not one with which I am particularly familiar, but I saw a series of documents which included things like this at different times. But as I say, not one I am particularly familiar with. Although I might point out, on looking at it now, that this document refers to mobilisation for Tactical Group I which was at a later date than the information about which I was just making reference, which is the number -- which was the people in the old Territorial Defence forces in Konjic prior to the onset of armed hostilities. So, to be clear, here you are talking about a phase once you have got to the formation of tactical groups and mobilisation for them and what I was saying before and what you asked me about was pertinent to the Territorial Defence within Bosnia and Herzegovina prior to the onset of armed hostilities, let us say, to the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So, within that framework, you need to be clear about what exactly it is we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would in fact like to talk about this given your comments. You said in this chart where it says, "Konjic", it is the very number that you referred to that is being mentioned, so Dr. Gow, my question to you is, in regard to this mobilisation chart, is this the chart -- was this chart part of your preparation for this -- for your testimony and is this one of the documents on the basis of which you talked about the tactical groups in the area in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is not a document on which I based my comments reference the fact that there were supposed to be 2,000 people in the Territorial Defence in Konjic, thereabouts. It is not a document upon which I have relied in any particular sense in any course of giving evidence, but it is part of a bundle of documents which have been shown to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You certainly must have taken into account this document in addition to other documents when you gave, when you offered your conclusions about what a tactical group may be. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not when I offered my conclusions about what a tactical group might be. In forming comments regarding the formation of tactical groups in this area, yes, but not regarding what a tactical group might be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you are familiar with Mr. Delalic's statement which also stated things that are reflected in this chart, I would now like to offer this document as a defence exhibit on the basis of Dr. Gow's general statements regarding this particular area of questioning. Is the exhibit admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, what actually is it supposed to portray? What do you want it to say? Because it is not an admission that his opinion was based on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We accept a series of documents from the UN resolutions to some other documents which have all assisted the witness to form his opinions. Dr. Gow has seen these documents among other documents. He also read Mr. Delalic's statement in which he explained this chart and this all formed the basis for his understanding of the tactical group and its role in the region, and so in that context I would like to offer it as a defence exhibit, since from here we can glean certain relevant aspects of what the tactical group was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we object to this document being tendered, certainly under the present basis, because it is an enormous leap to go from this document to an UN Resolution and say that because an UN Resolution has been admitted into evidence, this document should be admitted into evidence. We have no idea of its authorship, and Dr. Gow in his testimony has said that he has not relied on it in order to form the opinions that he has expressed. Now, it seems to us, your Honours, that if you give a document to a witness and he says, "Well, I have not relied on that", and then say, "Well, I wish to tender it", well, that is an inappropriate basis on which to tender it, so at the moment we object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: But this is a document supplied by you to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is not a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is what Ms. Residovic said. It was one of the documents supplied to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I do not know where she bases it. I have no idea where she gets that from. It may be a document which the Defence has given to the Prosecution and Dr. Gow may have seen it but it is not a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I am relying essentially on what the witness said. He did not rely on this document in forming his opinion. It is not admitted. I accept the interpretation did not bring that out clearly, but that was what I heard him say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I please -- is this a definitive decision or can we argue it a bit further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know what else you would argue. If you are relying on the fact that it was what he relied upon for his opinion, and he said no, he did not rely on this for his opinion, I do not know what your argument then is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding of the witness was, and I would like your assistance, the witness did not rely on this document when clarifying the general term of tactical groups, but if I understood you correctly, and Dr. Gow, please correct me if I am wrong, you also took it into account, this document, when you offered your general opinions about the area and in the given period of time, and since Mr. Delalic offered us the same -- the very same comments when -- that you referred to, so my understanding was that this document must have been part of the documents that you based your opinions on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that what I said in the first instance was that I was not immediately familiar, or especially familiar with this document. It was not one which immediately I recognised. I later said -- was the first part of what I said registered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But later you recognised it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I want to be clear that if the first part -- the microphone was not on when I spoke first. It came on when I was speaking. I want to check that the first part of what I said was registered, or should I begin again? Okay. Thank you. That the document was not one particularly familiar to me, that I had seen documents of which this might have been one which have some of the same broad type of information, that I did not rely on the document, either in forming my opinions about what a tactical group might be, or, I think I was trying to make clear, particularly in forming my views on the tactical group in this area. In response to your question I said that there is no way that I could, I think what I was trying to convey was that there was no way in which I could use it to form an opinion on what a tactical group might be, but that if, and I have to say "if", because I could not confirm for sure that it was one of these documents, I just assume that if these are the documents which are going around which I am being shown it was part of that set of documents, then in a small sense presumably I would have reviewed it, but going back to the original answer it was not something which I primarily relied on in forming my views, so I do not know where that leaves things.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, can you please, looking at this document, tell me whether this is a document which in contents relates to questions of mobilisation for Tactical Group 1, that is my first question, and that the document refers to the mobilisation for Tactical Group I. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can, and that is so. I think I already said that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to say, Dr. Gow, that from this table which is indicative of the mobilisation for Tactical Group I that we can clearly see that from the Konjic area, 300 soldiers are being mobilised for Tactical Group I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The way this scheme appears that would seem to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This scheme also shows how many soldiers are being mobilised for the tactical group from other municipalities for the area of operations of Tactical Group I.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would appear to show that as well, although I am not clear when you talk about mobilisation for the tactical group what you infer the document to show. It could be that these are people specifically being mobilised into units which exist already, because within the idea of tactical -- a tactical group you would be using existing units which would be assigned to a tactical group commander for a particular task. Now, there may be an element of strengthening those units by adding. It is not clear to me what this document represents, is what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look at the Konjic area for Tactical Group I? It is indicated that 300 soldiers should come under Tactical Group 1, and that 300 out of the 2,000 remain under the authority of the municipal staff of Konjic. You find this in the remark of the IV Corps which says that the body of the forces remains in the municipal staffs and are fully responsible to the main staff of the army, and partly to the war presidencies of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That may be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in view of the fact that the document is relevant in content for the questions we are discussing, and also due to the fact that Dr. Gow has among others reviewed this document, and from the standpoint of the relevance of this document that we should know which are the troops subordinated to Tactical Group 1, I would ask that this exhibit be admitted into evidence, as a defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose you can, but not on the ground that Dr. Gow has reviewed it, because he has done nothing of the sort. May I be following you in interpreting it as you went along? It does not originate from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: ... and you have to cross it also before you can get in the evidence. Who prepared this document and when was it prepared? It bears some sort of a seal on the original, but whose document is it? You already asked him to comment on it. Is it proven?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have to show provenance. You have to show us, from where does the document come, who prepared it and when was it prepared?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is an official document of the IV Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As far as I am able to recognise the signature, it is signed by Brigadier Mustafa Polutak --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The IV Corps was formed some time in November, so this document must have been prepared in November 1992. You are talking about the composition of the November 1992. What corps? If I remember correctly was formed some time in November 1992. This document comes from that corps, it must have been prepared after November 1992. It shows the composition then, not on the day it appeared, when we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually you do not give evidence of --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I answer? On the basis of the Defence investigation, on the basis of the official request of the Defence in 1996, addressed to the IV Corps, which has inherited all the units from the area in which the tactical group operated. The Defence received this document officially, as a structure of the IV Corps and in 1996 this document, together with official explanations, was given to the Prosecution, and during the interview with Mr. Delalic on 23rd August in Scheveningen was used by the Prosecutor during that interview. Therefore, the document was drafted in 1996, according to the documentation of the IV Corps, but it relates to the situation in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, might I...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually the problem is how does this witness tender it. You could not tender it through him, from all you have even said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the fact that this witness has analysed all the documents, including the interview in Scheveningen in which Delalic commented on this document in the presence of the Prosecutor, and that this was one of a series of documents that he reviewed in forming an opinion, and I am tendering it because of its relevance for the question we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: -- opinion. He said that he did not do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If you will not admit it, the only thing I can do is to continue with my cross-examination of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You can prove it is part of your defence document later on telling us from which source it comes and you can prove it, not that we are going to throw it out like this. You can prove it. It will be open to you when your defence case starts to prove this document from the records of the IV Corps. -- to speak about the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am very glad that we have come back to the question of authenticity because it seems to me that there was a period of time when much of the evidence was admitted on the basis of relevance, but I abide by your decision, and if the Defence is in that situation, it will prove this document, but I certainly hope that my client will not need that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually it is not lost to you. You can always tender it through your own witness. It would be easy.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I understand that, your Honours. I am hoping that we will not need any witnesses of our own. Dr. Gow, I should now like to ask you to try and bring to a close this conversation, and to ask you, would you agree with me that the municipal staffs of Territorial Defence and the corps later on, also formed tactical groups for the execution of certain occasional tactical combat tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what you have in mind in posing that particular question. I can provide two answers relevant to how I understand something, but I am not sure what it is to understand. The first is, as we have discussed several times, tactical groups were formed and at one stage the unusual step was taken of transforming a tactical group from the conventional understanding of specifically-assigned units for specific tasks to being all units for a particular area, and the way I read this in terms of the formation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina is that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I think that you did not understand my question well. I know what you said in that connection during the examination-in-chief. I do apologise, but my question is, are you aware that the municipal staffs, later on brigades and corps, also according to your knowledge, did form tactical groups for certain specific combat assignments. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, coming to the second part of what I was going to say, I said there were two interpretations I could put. The second would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Excuse me, please, why do you not take the questions as they are asked? Are you aware of the fact that local forces formed tactical groups?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was merely indicating that that is what I was proceeding to do, which is to say that it would be perfectly normal, again, for tactical units specifically to be formed for specific tactical purposes, and that I am aware that at later stages, both tactical groups and operational groups were formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Tactical groups and operational groups are the same, are they not? Most generally. Whenever a task is given to a particular group, it operates to achieve that objective.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Generally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, within general military thinking, it is possible to conceive of action, an activity at a strategic level, or even at a grand strategic level, or at a strategic level, at the operational level and at the tactical level. The three levels connote the degree to which you are working to a specific localised objective. When we are talking about tactical groups, we are talking about small groups, perhaps in this case comprising up to five components, possibly up to brigade size, and if you are talking at an operational level then you are talking about a much larger-scale operation over a wider spread of territory and involving a much larger number of units, so I think, I mean, what I am making the distinction of saying is that yes, both are designed to meet specific needs, but the level at which you are discussing things is different. So the tactical level would be specifically more or less local, an operational group would have a much broader range of operations. I hope that is clear. I am not sure... thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, Dr. Gow, if you could answer very clearly, my question. Are you aware that in that period, that is between April and November 1992, on the basis of your knowledge, that the municipal staffs and the brigades and later corps when they were formed, also formed tactical groups for the execution of specific combat tasks. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Concretely I am aware of the formation of the tactical groups 1 and 2 which we have discussed previously. I am not aware of any specific formations of tactical groups which municipal -- at a municipal level. I would be surprised other than in a very narrow sense that that would happen, but I would not exclude the possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned Tactical Group II. Tactical Group II was also formed by the main staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the same assignment as for Tactical Group I. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know that that tactical group was also active in the area of Igman, Hadzici, Pazaric and Trnovo. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that the area of Hadzici and Trnovo was an area which, before the war, and in the initial stages of the war, belonged to the district staff of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say I know, I would have to check, but I am prepared to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Later, when the I Corps was formed, this was an area that came under the responsibility of the I Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, yes. I would have to check all the places again, but yes. It is that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the previous question that I put to you I should like the witness to be shown an Exhibit D125/A/1. In view of the fact that it is an exhibit that has already been admitted into evidence, and that it is an exhibit of the Prosecution, I assume that in the selection of documents given to you by the OTP you also were able to review this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My first rule is always, "assume nothing", but anyway...

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen this document before, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure. I mean, I presume, again, in the mountain of documents, I may well have looked at it as I have been going through, but again it is not one to which I have paid a great deal of attention or upon which I have sought to rely for anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this is an exhibit tendered into evidence, you can see that it is a document issued on the 25th June 1992 by the army staff of Konjic, and that it is signed by the commander of the municipal staff, Esad Ramic. Is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That appears to be the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you look at the contents you are able to infer from it that the municipal staff formed as many as five tactical groups for the conduct of battle in the direction of the Boras Lake and on the basis of an order by the republican commander of the army of the 18th June 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that the circulation list includes coordinators, an interesting use of word, of five tactical groups within this area. I am not entirely clear to what the document refers, because it is quite clearly outside the framework of the tactical groups organised to which we have made reference earlier, Tactical Group I and Tactical Group II for the specific operations, although it seems to relate to the same kinds of operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you were clear. This is quite different because it relates to a previous period, and in an area east of Konjic towards the mountain of Pren and the Boracko Lake. This operation is obviously being conducted by the municipal staff. My question was simply for you to confirm that the municipal staff in the conduct of these operations did form tactical groups itself for specific tasks, and that is, I think, what we can adduce from this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would be prepared to agree that the document designates five tactical groups, presumably under the command of the Konjic army headquarters, in which the circulation goes to coordinator and the coordinators of the tactical groups which, in the context of this and in fact of our earlier discussions must be taken to mean people who are regarded as having command responsibility in those situations, but I would note that the date, 25th June 1992 is also in the period that Tactical Group I has already been formed and I think by then Tactical Group II on the larger scale we have been talking about so it is not an earlier period. It is within the same period, so I think we can be clear, yes, the designation is used, the term, "coordinator", is used for those people charged with responsibility for them; again, a flexible situation but it is in the same period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This document can be returned to the Registry. Finally, Dr. Gow, before I thank you, I should like you to confirm my conclusions from this very fatiguing testimony for you, I am sure. You have actually based your opinion on Konjic on general knowledge of the circumstances, and the documents given to you by the Office of the Prosecutor in preparation for this testimony. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have said many times, I have based it -- I bring my general understanding and expertise to bear and in reviewing documents, I select those which it seems to me add to the understanding regarding Konjic, and where that marries with the general expertise, but I think I said a long time ago at the beginning of the evidence I skimmed many, many documents but I could not possibly -- I could not say I have examined all of them in detail, I just looked through to try and find things which were useful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as my final point, you personally did not do any kind of research in Konjic, nor did you verify the authenticity of the documents that you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have confirmed that I do not think I have ever been to Konjic. If I did pass through sometime, I did not realise that I was doing so, and that I think I said also that I did not personally verify documents. I did not see it as my responsibility to verify documents. I used documents on the basis either that they have already been accepted or, as I have said on other occasions, that they have been evaluated by well-qualified experts on behalf of member governments for the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, I wish to thank you, Dr. Gow, and if you know any of my friends, please convey my greetings when you get to London. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much Ms. Residovic. Any other questions from... any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I only have one question, your Honour. Dr. Gow, Mr. Ackerman, when he was cross-examining you, asked you a number of questions and showed you documents in relation to the withdrawal of the JNA which later became the VJ from Bosnia and Herzegovina in May of 1992. Notwithstanding those documents and what you said about this withdrawal, was there still the continued involvement of the JNA or the VJ in Bosnia and Herzegovina after May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was. I believe that I have already indicated in testimony that the -- that at that initial stage JNA continued to be identified as being present in Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is personnel from Serbia and Montenegro who had not yet been withdrawn for some time afterwards that the whole operation of the army of the Republika Srpska was, in fact, a JNA/Belgrade military operation, but by that stage, as proxies, because of this -- what is described as Communist approach of deception, so as not to be identified, the attempt to avoid being identified as Belgrade being responsible for the operations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we made reference to the evidence from the diary of Bosislav Jovic that that decision was taken at the end of 1991 specifically with a view to a situation in which they knew they would be regarded as an external power, and trying to avoid that designation, and in addition to that, I think in evidence at other times in Tadic and in other cases I have made reference to a number of occasions where even after the formal division and in spite of this attempt to maintain the idea that there were two separate armies, a number of cases in which the VJ itself did participate, or is known to have participated, and I think this is on record, for example, the air operations in 1994 which involved personnel from Podgorica and Montenegro, the introduction of special forces from Nis and Ordica in the course of a number of actions including those at Gorazde in 1994, the insertion of reinforcement troops, perhaps as many as 4,000 through the Posafina Corridor at various stages, so there are a number of instances, openly-known instances in which the VJ itself was obliged, covertly but sometimes being disclosed to contribute, and of course I would go back to the position I made reference to on Friday, the report of Ambassador Pardue, the US special representative for arms control in Bosnia in the Former Yugoslavia territories, that one of the problems with the army of the Republika Srpska is that it still has these ties to Belgrade so they are not dealing all the time with an army there but with something which is tied to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that is the end of the case of the Prosecution, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was going to close the case, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the end of your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was going to close it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much Dr. Gow. You have been very helpful, and I am sure the Defence also have been fairly satisfied with your answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I certainly hope so. It took a long time to get there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I said, "fairly". I did not say "fully". So, we thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, your Honour, that is the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Now, I think on the 12th we had an undertaking from the Defence that you intend to make a submission, and that within three days of the close of the Prosecution case -- do you still abide by that promise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to be able to file by 1 o'clock on Friday, if that would be okay with the Trial Chamber and in line with that that adds maybe a half a day to what we had in mind, but it appears now that we need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution will not grudge you even if you file it on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But we will file at 1 o'clock on Friday, then, that is what we will plan to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Olujic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before this decision is taken, the Defence of the second accused, Zdravko Mucic would like to appeal to the Trial Chamber, given the statement by Dr. Gow on Friday and today. We would like an extension of this deadline, that is until the end of the month, that is the 28th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see Ms. Residovic wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, but a completely different issue from the one that we just -- from the issue that we were just discussing, so maybe we should wait for your decision on this issue first and then I will indulge you to hear me out on the issue that I have to bring up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I was relying on your undertaking to be able to file it within the week, and that is Friday the 20th. I thought that was sufficient. I did not know, even, that Dr. Gow added anything to what he would have said, even if he did not come again it would not have made much of a difference to your case. Well, I thought that you should be able to abide by that undertaking. I hear Mr. Olujic saying something different, the end of the month. That is a week after. Well, I do not know. That is a little different from what we both understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Delalic Defence accepts the deadline of Friday, 1 pm, but I would like to ask a question on another issue. This could be my mistake, maybe not, but in preparation for the cross-examination of Dr. Gow I have looked through the exhibits proffered by the Prosecutor, including the Delalic statement from Scheveningen, the Exhibits 997 and 998 was admitted. It includes a report on the conditions in Celebici. This was introduced through Witness D, and this was admitted to the -- into evidence, but I would like to state that it is inconceivable that this exhibit should be attached, or admitted with the Delalic statement, so I want to ask that it be separated out from this exhibit. Zejnil Delalic said that he never heard or saw this person, and given the -- and this report is part of his statement given in Scheveningen, the detention unit, and this is how these documents were presented to us by the Prosecution, and we would like this particular document to be taken out of this bundle. He has never seen it. He does not know about it and this document does not belong with the Exhibits 99/7 and 99/8. The other thing that I want to bring up is just a clarification on whether I understood you correctly, something from the transcript, and that is that the statements of the co-accused cannot be used against the other co-accused. If this is correct I would like you to confirm it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, I suppose there might be some confusion here, and perhaps you are not familiar with the procedure of a no-case submission. That is one other thing. It appears when you are making a no-case submission, you are arguing that no prima facie case has been made against your client for the Trial Chamber to call him to come and give his own side of the story. Now, all the arguments on that basis are arguments of law. If you have arguments based on evidence simply, simplicita, perhaps you are using a different argument, although nobody stops you arguing that you are closing your case with that of the Prosecution, if you want to do so. If you want to take the chance, and to make a submission both on law and the evidence, you can do so, and take the chance of either succeeding or failing on that and no longer going forward to give evidence, so there are two sides of it. If you are making a no-case submission, the submission is based entirely on legal grounds. I think this is our understanding of a no-case submission. Now, when you start questioning the weight of evidence and other matters which are not strictly based on law, you are going beyond the ambit of a no-case submission and might not be acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that we had a complete misunderstanding. Obviously I was not very clear on what I intended to say. When I say that the Defence may not find it necessary for me to give evidence, that is based on the fact that the Delalic Defence is claiming that their client is innocent, but if this request is not accepted, we will obviously call witnesses and offer evidence. What I am doing here is -- I am doing as a professional and I am following the -- what my client is telling me. However, there is -- what I have addressed here is something else. We say that there was an error made in the exhibit that were submitted here in 99/7 and 8. In other words, my client says that he has never stated things that were -- that appeared in Exhibit 99/7 and 99/8. This was later introduced through another witness, and this is an error that could be a technical error, it is something that can be corrected, and this is what I was referring to when I touched on this subject, and the other thing is, whether I have understood your position correctly, because we had not received a written decision, so I need to be perfectly clear about whether you intend to use the statements of the accused against the other co-accused provided they do not appear here as witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Well, as far as this Trial Chamber is concerned, I do not know what happens elsewhere, we do not give hypothetical decisions, decisions which are likely to come when, in fact, they might not even come. Now, according to our law here, what you have been doing, we have always said that the evidence of an accused person, the statement of an accused person is only evidence against himself, not against another accused person, so that even if it was tendered it has nothing to do with another accused person, except it was admitted by that accused person, and then it forms part of the statement as a whole, in which case it will apply to the other accused person. As long as you have the position which no such statement has been tendered for the purposes for which it is being -- evidence is being led, you do not have any fear. So you do not expect us to give a decision against somebody who might, in future, object to it. Now, if there is any attempt to use it against another accused person, obviously you will object to it, and even if you do not, as common-law judges we will do it ourselves, because we know that it should not be evidence against the other accused person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have one scheduling problem I ought to bring to the court's attention, something probably more for the Registry, but as I understand the schedule that we are all agreed on, we are going to file something by 1 o'clock on Friday. The Prosecutor would then have two weeks, which would be Friday, March 6th, and we agreed that we would have a week to respond to that which would make it like, I think, March 11th -- no, Friday of the next week, in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the Trial Chamber is scheduled to meet during that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: On the 11th and 12th we should be meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and the question I have is that if we have not completed our response to their -- our reply to their response to our submission, I do not know what we can do. It might be to everyone's advantage if we could trade off some days with another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will see what we can do, whether we can find a way of you shortening your time, and coming within the period of -- we will find out something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, the problem I see with that, Judge, is that if they file it on March 6th, Friday, March 6th, I am not likely to have it until Monday, March 8th, have it in my hands, or March 9th, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It leaves only one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That creates a problem, so I just wanted to point that out to the court and see if we can in some amicable way solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We will find a way of trying to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, of course, your Honour, if Mr. Niemann files a week early that solves the whole problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am very grateful for that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So, hopefully, we accept these dates, except, I do not know, Mr. Olujic, are you falling in line or are you still staying the odd man out?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we requested of you, if you could meet our needs, given the consultations that I also had with my client with regard to the -- Dr. Gow's testimony, so we will abide by your decisions anyway, because your decision is law for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We are trying to find that everybody falls in line and facilitates the argument. It makes life easier for both the Prosecution and the Defence. I am trying to turn to the Prosecution for assistance to see if they can file two days earlier. Can you? (Pause).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no idea what we are going to get. We have tried to anticipate what we are going to get, but for us to sort of say now yes, we can do it two days earlier is really very difficult, and all we can say is we could try, but I think that we would have to find some other means of perhaps seeing whether Registry can send it over by courier or something of that nature. We might be able to accommodate and assist in that way, but at this stage, we just cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You have got a very able team!

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think, let us remain in constant consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: So that whatever happens, we know how to adjust it. So let us keep the date as it is, and remain in constant consultation to be able to arrange it. So thank you very much. I think we are on our first lap. The Trial Chamber will now adjourn.
